speaker: Drago Anguelov
title: Inside Waymo's New Foundation Model Powering Self-Driving Cars [Drago Anguelov]
question: In autonomous driving, what is the core trade-off between training models to predict future raw sensor observations versus predicting driving trajectories?
guest: Predicting driving trajectories is the most topical signal for how you should drive—you observe how people drive and learn to predict those motion tokens. A next level is predicting other people's motion tokens jointly around you, so you model how everyone else reacts to you and how you react to them. Now, going to sensors is the highest-bandwidth prediction you have—all the information you actually have about the future. You're dreaming the full environment in its full fidelity, including how objects look from the other side, how reflections work, and how LiDAR intensity relates to RGB pixels. But the issue is, are you overdoing it? As a human driver, I don't spend my time thinking about how a tree looks from the other side, how branches occlude each other, or how a shadow evolves on a pedestrian. While there is a lot of knowledge inherent in the sensors, not all of it is relevant to driving. Predicting what people do a few steps ahead is the most topical, and as you broaden, it becomes increasingly less relevant—like modeling how clouds move in the sky. It can be helpful for a simulator to model that, but it doesn't always help you drive.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core trade-off is between the richness of the supervision signal and its relevance to the driving task.

Predicting future raw sensor observations (video frames, LiDAR point clouds) gives dense, self-supervised training signal from unlabeled data at massive scale. This forces the model to learn general world dynamics: scene geometry, how other agents move, and physical causality. The cost is that most of that capacity and compute goes to modeling details irrelevant to driving decisions, such as textures, foliage, clouds and sensor noise. It is expensive, and good pixel reconstruction does not guarantee good planning.

Predicting trajectories directly is compact, cheap and aligned with what actually matters: the driving action. But the supervision is sparse and low-dimensional, a handful of waypoints per scene, typically requiring expert demonstrations or labels. Models can therefore learn shortcuts (for example, extrapolating ego-motion), exhibit causal confusion, and generalize poorly to rare situations because they are never forced to understand the scene deeply.

This is why many recent approaches combine the two: using observation or latent-space future prediction as a pretraining or auxiliary objective to build representations, then training or fine-tuning with trajectory objectives for task-focused planning.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
The core trade-off is between representational richness with scalable self-supervision, and computational efficiency with direct task alignment.

Predicting future raw sensor observations, such as camera pixels or LiDAR point clouds, preserves complete scene context—capturing unmodeled obstacles, surface conditions, and subtle visual cues without hand-crafted abstractions—while enabling self-supervised learning across massive, unlabeled driving logs. However, raw sensor streams are high-dimensional and stochastic, forcing models to spend vast capacity and inference compute reconstructing driving-irrelevant details like clouds or roadside foliage, without directly producing vehicle controls.

Conversely, predicting driving trajectories concentrates computation on compact, low-dimensional outputs directly usable for real-time planning and control, ignoring irrelevant background variance. Yet compressing complex scenes into sparse coordinates creates an information and supervision bottleneck: trajectories provide weak training signal per sample for learning general world dynamics, discard semantic context needed for rare long-tail hazards, and leave models prone to causal confusion or reliant on costly perception annotations.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The core trade-off is **rich, scalable supervision versus task relevance and efficiency**.

Training a model to predict future raw sensor data, such as camera frames or LiDAR sweeps, gives it a dense, self-supervised signal. Every pixel or point acts as a label, so the model can learn from huge amounts of unlabeled driving logs and pick up detailed scene dynamics and physics. The cost is that much of its capacity and compute goes into reconstructing details that don't matter for driving, like textures, lighting, sky and foliage. High-fidelity prediction is also expensive, and good reconstruction doesn't reliably lead to better decisions, because the model still has to turn its predictions into actions.

Predicting trajectories directly is aligned with the actual goal and is cheap to train and run. But the signal is sparse: just a few waypoints per scene, usually taken from expert demonstrations. That makes the model hungry for labeled data and prone to shortcuts, such as extrapolating from the car's own speed instead of reading the scene. It also suffers from causal confusion and generalizes poorly to rare situations.

Current research often aims for a middle ground. It predicts future states in a compact latent feature space rather than raw pixels, and uses that as an auxiliary objective alongside trajectory planning.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: The core trade-off is between rich, self-supervised environmental representation and direct, efficient alignment with the control objective. Training models to predict future raw sensor observations—such as camera frames or LiDAR sweeps—leverages massive unlabeled driving data to learn dense scene dynamics, physics, and long-tail phenomena without relying on brittle hand-crafted abstractions. However, this approach is computationally expensive and spends significant capacity modeling task-irrelevant details like textures, lighting, and background clutter, while still requiring an additional step to translate predictions into driving actions. Conversely, predicting driving trajectories directly optimizes a compact, low-dimensional output aligned with planning and control, making models faster, easier to verify, and better suited for real-time execution. The downside is a much sparser supervision signal that can struggle to generalize to rare scenarios, miss subtle environmental cues, and suffer from causal confusion or overfitting to biases in expert demonstrations. Consequently, modern systems increasingly combine both paradigms, using world-model pretraining or latent prediction to inform trajectory planning.

Predicting future camera frames or lidar scans gives a model a rich training signal about how the whole scene evolves. But raw observations are high-dimensional, and the model can spend substantial compute predicting details like lighting and texture that rarely change a driving decision.

Predicting trajectories focuses the model on where the ego vehicle or other road users could move. That output is cheaper to model and easier for a planner to use, but it provides less supervision about the scene and can omit cues that matter in unfamiliar situations. The trade-off is richer supervision about the world versus a more compact prediction aligned with driving decisions.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Predicting future camera frames or lidar scans teaches a model how the scene may evolve. It can learn from raw driving logs without labeled maneuvers, but it spends capacity and compute on details that may have little bearing on the next driving decision. A planner still has to turn those predictions into actions.

Predicting the vehicle’s trajectory focuses learning directly on where to drive. The output is compact and easier for a controller to use, but a recorded trajectory shows only the path one driver took. On its own, it provides less supervision about how the surrounding scene might evolve or what would happen along another path. The trade-off is between learning a richer, more general model of the world and learning a more efficient, task-specific model of driving behavior.
